title: Metformin and reduced vitamin B12 levels: new advice for monitoring patients at risk
authors: Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency
journal: Drug Safety Update volume 15, issue 11, June 2022: 1, published 20 June 2022
funder: Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency
result: Decreased vitamin B12 levels, or vitamin B12 deficiency, is now considered a common adverse drug reaction of metformin. After a European review of the brand leader Glucophage with MHRA input, the product information was updated to state that vitamin B12 deficiency is common and may affect up to 1 in 10 people who take it, and that the risk increases with higher dose, longer treatment duration and pre-existing risk factors. The agency advises testing serum vitamin B12 when deficiency is suspected, for example in patients presenting with megaloblastic anaemia or new-onset neuropathy, considering periodic monitoring in patients with risk factors, and continuing metformin while the deficiency is corrected. The mechanism is described as multifactorial, comprising altered intestinal motility, bacterial overgrowth and reduced uptake of vitamin B12 in the small intestine. Patients with deficiency can be asymptomatic or present with megaloblastic anaemia, neuropathy or both; other features include depression, irritability, cognitive impairment, glossitis, mouth ulcers and visual and motor disturbances, and the statement notes that anaemia or neuropathy caused by deficiency should be diagnosed and treated as soon as possible to avoid permanent symptoms. Listed risk factors: baseline B12 at the lower end of the normal range; conditions reducing absorption, including older age, total or partial gastrectomy, Crohn's disease and other inflammatory bowel disorders and autoimmune conditions; diets low in B12 such as strict vegan and some vegetarian diets; concomitant medicines impairing B12 absorption, including proton pump inhibitors and colchicine; and genetic predisposition such as Imerslund-Grasbeck syndrome and transcobalamin II deficiency. The four cited references are Aroda 2016, Beulens 2015, de Jager 2010 and Miller 2018.
